title: Who Pays for Unions? - Marginal REVOLUTION
gist: A forthcoming QJE study by Dodini, Stansbury and Willén uses Norwegian union-dues tax-deductibility changes as quasi-exogenous variation in firm-level union density and finds unionization mostly redistributes from consumers via higher prices rather than from shareholders, with effects flipping sign by market structure: competitive private-sector firms contract employment and lose profits, while less-competitive manufacturing firms expand employment and protect margins by passing costs through.

themes.theme: Union cost incidence falls on consumers, not shareholders

insights.claim: In Norwegian data, unionization primarily redistributes from consumers through higher prices rather than from shareholders through lower profits, inverting the standard labor-versus-capital framing of union bargaining.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Union-density shocks should be modeled as a pricing/inflation pass-through channel first and an equity-margin channel second — screen consumer-facing pricing power, not just labor cost lines.
insights.quote: Overall, unionization in this setting primarily redistributes from consumers rather than shareholders

insights.claim: Incidence of higher union-driven labor costs is split three ways — consumer prices, shareholder profits, and productivity improvements that offset the remainder — so no single stakeholder absorbs the full shock.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Use a three-way incidence split rather than a binary wage-versus-margin assumption when stress-testing labor-cost shocks in earnings models.
insights.quote: The incidence is shared: consumers bear part of the cost through higher prices, shareholders through lower profits, and the remainder is offset by productivity improvements.

themes.theme: Market structure flips the sign of the union effect

insights.claim: Firm responses to unionization vary systematically with the degree of product- and labor-market competition, meaning the same union shock produces opposite employment outcomes across sectors.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Sector concentration is the key conditioning variable for forecasting how labor policy hits employment and margins — do not apply one economy-wide multiplier.
insights.quote: Firm responses vary systematically by the degree of market competition.

insights.claim: In the average private sector firm, higher union density raises labor costs and causes firms to contract employment and production, lowering profits without raising the labor share.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Rising union density in competitive sectors is a double negative — headcount contraction plus profit compression — with no offsetting labor-share gain to justify it.
insights.quote: higher union density raises labor costs and leads firms to contract employment and production, lowering profits without increasing the labor share
insights.locator: In the average private sector firm

insights.claim: In manufacturing, where product and labor markets are less competitive, higher union density reverses the standard result: the average firm expands employment and production, reduces labor markdowns, and suffers no profit decline.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Manufacturing unionization is not automatically a margin threat — in concentrated markets it can raise output and wages while leaving profits intact.
insights.quote: In manufacturing, where firms operate in less competitive product and labor markets, the response is reversed

insights.claim: Unions can offset employer monopsony power, so who bears the cost of unionization depends importantly on the underlying market structure rather than on union strength alone.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: In monopsonistic labor markets, union gains can be efficiency-enhancing rather than purely extractive — a rebuttal to blanket anti-union cost modeling.
insights.quote: unions can offset employer monopsony power

insights.claim: The total wage bill falls under higher union density, with losses concentrated among less-attached “outsider” workers rather than spread evenly across the workforce.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Union wage gains for insiders come at the expense of marginal workers — expect labor-market dualization, not uniform wage inflation, after union-strengthening policy.
insights.quote: The total wage bill falls, with losses concentrated among less-attached “outsider” workers.

insights.claim: Unionization drives a reallocation of activity toward larger and more productive firms, implying industry consolidation as a second-order consequence of labor policy.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Pro-union policy shifts is a relative tailwind for scaled incumbents and a headwind for subscale competitors — a consolidation trade, not just a cost story.
insights.quote: including a reallocation toward larger and more productive firms

insights.claim: Changes in the tax deductibility of union dues in Norway provide quasi-exogenous variation in firm-level union density, giving a credible identification strategy for causal union effects.
insights.speaker: Tyler Cowen
insights.so_what: Tax-code tweaks to dues deductibility are an under-watched policy lever that measurably moves union density — worth tracking in other jurisdictions.
insights.quote: using changes in the tax deductibility of union dues in Norway as a quasi-exogenous source of variation in firm-level union density
